title: Gouache Storybook
subject: fun
style: An opaque-gouache picture book, animated: every shape is a flat, opaque patch of paint that carries its own brush direction, a few black dry-brush marks give it drawing, and the scenes change by being PAINTED ON (broad brush ribbons), by a push THROUGH a round window that holds another world, or by hard cuts on the beat. This is gouache, not watercolour or ink wash: no washes, no bleeding, no gradients, no transparency in the paint; value comes from a second flat shape, never from a blend. THE CADENCE (the reference's measured tell): the film is 24 fps but every fourth picture is held, so there are 18 new paintings a second. Every animated quantity reads the painted time T(F) = i − (i mod 4 == 1 ? 1 : 0) with i = floor(F), never F itself; cuts, ribbons' start frames and sound cues stay on F (cuts and cues sit on the 12-frame beat and ribbons start on multiples of 4, so a cut or a new ribbon is never a held frame). still-frames.mjs will count about a quarter of frames 'identical': that is the design, and no half-second window is ever still. No motion blur (paint is crisp); the one exception is the push through the glass (below). PAPER: the ground colour with a paper-tooth tile computed ONCE per size into an offscreen canvas (seeded: about 12,000 specks of 1–2 px in line and surface at 4–8% alpha, plus a low-frequency mottle), drawn over the finished frame at 6% so every scene sits on the same sheet. THE BRISTLE TILE, also computed once per size (512 × 512, seeded): about 900 thin strokes all running along +x, 1–3 px wide, 60–400 px long, slightly curved, alternately surface and ink at 3–9% alpha, with ragged ends: a colour-neutral streak map. A PAINTED SHAPE is: its outline sampled every ~12 px with each vertex pushed in or out by seeded noise of 0–3 px at 1080 (never vector-perfect); a flat fill; then, clipped to the shape, the bristle tile drawn rotated to the shape's own brush angle (a fixed per-shape angle that follows the form: horizontal across a sky, down a coat, round a hat) plus two or three 'load' streaks of the fill mixed 25% with surface where the brush was fullest; and on the trailing side 6–20 drag hairs, thin streaks of the fill 10–40 px long leaving the edge along the brush angle (the dry-brush fringe). Textures are locked to their shapes: nothing boils, a held painting is a still painting. SHADING is two flat tones: each form gets one shadow shape (its fill darkened 18% and pulled 20% toward s5) on the side away from a fixed upper-left light, and a highlight dab of surface at 50–70% with streaks (cheek glint, the glass's arc). Blush is an s7 dab of five overlapping streaks at 35%. INK is accent, not outline: black dry-brush marks only on the shadow side of a form and on defining lines (the dot eyes, the hat's ribbing, window frames, roof edges, the globe's rim), and no contour closes: each covers 60–85% of its perimeter. An ink mark is a centreline with width w(s) = w0 · sin(πs)^0.5, rendered as 4–6 parallel sub-lines across that width whose visibility along s is gated by seeded 1D value noise, so the mark breaks into bristle streaks where the brush ran dry, mostly near its ends. THE PORTAL is a snow globe: a glass circle on a small wooden base (s3 trapezoid with a dark grain streak); its world is drawn in the circle's own unit space and clipped to it; the glass is a thin surface rim at 50%, one broad curved dry-brush highlight arc in surface at 70% upper left and a short reflection streak lower right, with the rim's ink mark on the shadow side. EVERY WORLD is one function world(k, box, T) with two passes, paint (the painted shapes) and ink (the dry-brush marks), so the same world can fill the frame behind the kid, sit small inside the globe as a preview, or be drawn ink-only as its underdrawing: that single source is what makes each match cut through the glass exact. Worlds are few-shape landscapes (sea with a striped lighthouse; mustard dunes and a white sun; layered viridian jungle fans; indigo night pines on snow with star dabs; an ultramarine reef with vermilion fish and bubble rings; night rooftops with mustard windows; a cratered grey moon on deep with a ringed planet; patchwork fields under striped balloons) and the kid's HOME: a slate street of narrow houses in drizzle. BRUSH RIBBONS (the wipe that paints the next scene on): a ribbon is a cubic Bézier centreline that runs past both frame edges, a width of 220–360 px at 1080, a start frame and a 20-frame sweep; head h(u) = easeInOut(u) along the curve, tail = max(0, h − 0.55); the ribbon polygon is the centreline offset ±W/2 between tail and head, its edges ragged by seeded 1D noise of 0–10 px, its head split into 4–6 dry bristle tongues, painted in the ribbon's colour with the bristle tile oriented along the tangent. The next world is drawn clipped to the union of every ribbon swept so far and the old world outside it; after the last ribbon clears, the new world is full frame. The unpaint runs the same machinery, revealing the ink-only pass on bare paper. SNOW: about 140 flakes inside the globe (about 220 full frame inside the globe world); flake i has seeds x0, y0, r (2–6 px), v, ω, φ: y = (y0 + v · T) mod h, x = x0 + A · sin(ω T + φ); each shake at frame t_k adds, for T > t_k, a swirl offset S · e^(−(T − t_k)/18) along a per-flake direction and a vortex rotation about the globe centre of 1.6 · (1 − e^(−(T − t_k)/8)) · e^(−(T − t_k)/40) rad: closed-form sums over the shakes already past, never a simulation. Flakes are surface-coloured dabs (small rotated ellipses with one streak), not glowing dots. RAIN: dry-brush dashes (1.5 px, 30–60 px, surface at 35%) on a seeded grid at 15° falling 26 px per painted frame, wrapped mod the frame height. THE KID (invented): a small kid in a mustard (s1) knitted hat with a vermilion pom-pom, an ultramarine (accent2) duffel coat with three surface toggles, a vermilion scarf, s6 skin, two ink dot eyes each with one surface glint, s7 blush dabs, a small ink mouth arc, mustard mittens. Built from separate painted parts, each with its own pivot (head, hat, pom-pom, scarf, torso, two two-segment arms, mittens, legs), drawn with ctx.save/translate/rotate from its parent; poses are keyed joint angles eased between keys; a 6 px head bob on every beat. Blink: the eyes' height × 0.1 for 4 frames. Eyes widen: scale 1 → 1.5 on a spring (about 12% overshoot). A shake jolt at t_k moves the globe by 26 · sin(2π(T − t_k)/6) · e^(−(T − t_k)/10) px vertically, the arms follow it, the pom-pom lags on a damped spring. The scarf streams in wind as a ribbon (same renderer as the wipes) whose centreline is a travelling sine, y = a(x) · sin(kx − ωT) with a growing along its length: hair-into-paint-stroke grammar, in a scarf. THE CAMERA is one transform over the world. The push through the glass and the pull back out are exponential about the globe's centre, scale = 14^ease(u), the globe centre travelling to the frame centre; once the globe's radius passes the frame's half-diagonal, draw the inside world full frame (the match cut). During the fastest 8 frames of each, add a radial zoom smear: three extra copies of the frame at ×0.96, ×0.92, ×0.88 about the fixed point at 25%, 15% and 8% alpha. Holds carry a slow 1.00 → 1.03 push and a 2 px sine drift, so no painting is ever frozen. THE IRIS: the outside of a circle is filled with deep, its radius closing from the frame's half-diagonal to the globe's radius + 30 px; its edge is painted, not geometric: the radius wobbles by seeded angular noise of ±6 px and about 40 dry-brush streaks of deep sweep tangentially across it. TYPE: one line in the whole film, the end title 'Shake for Elsewhere.' in Instrument Serif 400 at 120 px (landscape at 1080), surface on deep, fading up over 12 frames, no plate. Nothing else is written; the pictures carry the story.
learnsFrom: A painted animation shared on X by @Artedeingenio (https://x.com/Artedeingenio/status/2104618081029152958), 30 s at 24 fps: opaque gouache-look illustration with bristle-streaked flat fills and black dry-brush accents; pictures held one frame in four (18 new images a second); round portals that hold other worlds and match cuts THROUGH them; a centred, locked figure whose world hard-swaps behind it on the beat; broad paint ribbons that sweep across and repaint the scene; a moment where the colour drains to its ink drawing; and a brush-edged iris to black at the end. Its red-haired girl, her plaid shirt, trousers and sunglasses, the lenses as the portal, the seasons cycling on a suburban house, the eye in the sky and the town in the pupil, the wink and the eyelid close, its cadmium-orange, sage, powder-blue and pink colour set, its music and every one of its frames are not used; the kid, the snow globe, the worlds, the story and the title are invented.

story.what: hook: the camera is already right up against the globe's glass, which fills the frame edge to edge: a tiny vermilion-and-white striped lighthouse on a dark ultramarine sea, snow whirling in a slow vortex, the glass's white dry-brush highlight arcing across the top; at 12 the globe JOLTS (the whole picture kicks 40 px down and springs back, the snow bursts upward: a hit); at 24 a second, smaller jolt (a tick)

the pull-back (48–84, exponential out from the globe's centre): the glass shrinks into a snow globe held in two mustard mittens, the kid's face above it (mustard hat, vermilion pom-pom, ultramarine coat), and around them the HOME street: slate sky, narrow grey-blue houses, dry-brush drizzle; the globe is the only bright thing in the frame; the kid blinks at 84 (a tick)

the shake: three jolts on the beat (96, 108, 120, a tick each), the snow storming inside the glass, the pom-pom bouncing behind on its spring, cheeks puffed; at 132 the kid leans in and peers into the glass

the first repaint (a whoosh ends at 144): three broad ribbons, ultramarine, white and viridian, sweep left to right one after another (starting 144, 148, 152, 20 frames each), and wherever they pass the street is painted over by the globe's world at full size: horizon, sea with white wave dashes, the striped lighthouse, gull ticks in ink; the drizzle stops; the last ribbon clears at 172 (a hit on 168 as the lighthouse lands); the scarf streams out in the sea wind and the pom-pom flaps

close-up (a cut on 192): the kid's face and the globe fill the frame; inside the glass there is a NEW world now, mustard dunes under a white sun; the kid's eyes widen on a spring at 204 (a tick); two more jolts at 216 and 228 (ticks), snow churning over the dunes

the montage (drums enter on 240): the kid stands full figure, centred and locked, the globe held overhead in both mittens; the world behind HARD-CUTS on every beat, eight paintings in eight beats: dunes (240), jungle (252), night pines on snow (264), a reef under water (276), night rooftops (288), the moon with a ringed planet (300), balloon fields (312), and at 324 all of them at once in eight vertical bands; the globe always shows the NEXT world, so each cut is foretold; the kid cycles through three poses (a tick per cut)

through the glass (a hit on 336 ends the montage): the kid lowers the globe to the lens and the camera pushes into it, exponential about its centre (×14 over 336–380, with the radial smear on the fastest frames); the rim's ink mark and the highlight arc slide past the frame edges (a whoosh ends at 384)

inside the globe: a tiny round square with three narrow houses (vermilion, mustard and viridian doors) and one tree, snow drifting down; overhead, the curved glass horizon (a huge arc with a white dry-brush highlight) and beyond it the giant kid's face peering in, fish-eyed (radial remap r' = R · sin(πr / 2R)); at 432 the giant kid taps the glass (a hit): the whole little world jolts and the snow bursts up; at 456 the giant eyes blink (a tick)

the unpaint (a whoosh ends at 504): three ribbons sweep right to left and lift the colour off wherever they pass, leaving only the ink underdrawing, now with every contour closed, on bare paper; 504–516 the underdrawing holds on a slow push, the snow drawn as tiny ink circles
the repaint: new ribbons lay the colour back on, but as evening: indigo sky, mustard lit windows, the snow white again (a hit on 528 as the first ribbon crosses the middle)

back out (a whoosh ends at 552): the camera pulls out of the glass (the push reversed) to the kid in the HOME street, but the drizzle has stopped, the slate sky has turned peach at the horizon, puddles hold the lit windows, and a cap of snow sits on the kid's hat; the kid grins at 588 (a tick)

the kid lifts the globe toward the lens: inside it is the HOME street itself, with a tiny kid holding a tiny globe (one step deep, drawn once, never a loop); a highlight streak sweeps across the glass at 612 (a tick); at 636 the iris begins to close

the end (a whoosh ends at 648): the brush-edged iris closes onto the globe and the frame is deep black around it (a hit on 660); under it the title fades up, 'Shake for Elsewhere.' (from 672, with the sign-off); inside the glass the snow slowly settles over the tiny street, the last flake landing at 708 (a tick); a slow push-in keeps it alive to the last frame

sizes: Landscape (primary, 1920 × 1080): the kid's head and the globe share the centre for close-ups; in wide shots the kid stands just left of centre with the world opening to the right; ribbons sweep left to right across the long side; the montage figure is about 820 px tall; the end title sits on one line under the globe at 120 px. Vertical (1080 × 1920) re-stacks rather than crops: close-ups put the kid's face in the upper half and the globe held lower, larger (about 640 px across); the worlds are authored taller (the lighthouse taller, the jungle fans stacked, the rooftops climbing, the moon high in the frame); ribbons sweep diagonally from top left to bottom right so they cross the tall frame in the same 20 frames; the montage figure is about 1,300 px tall with the globe overhead in the top third; inside the globe, the giant face fills the upper half through the curved glass and the tiny square sits in the lower third; the end title breaks into two centred lines ('Shake for' / 'Elsewhere.') at 120 px under the globe. Every size keeps the title inside layout().safe.
sound: beatScore drive at 120 bpm, key 3, with the drums entering at the montage (drop 240); hits at 12 (the first jolt), 168 (the lighthouse lands), 336 (the montage ends), 432 (the giant tap), 528 (the repaint) and 660 (the iris closes); whooshes ending at 144 (the ribbons), 384 (through the glass), 504 (the unpaint), 552 (back out) and 648 (the iris); ticks at 24, 84, 96, 108, 120, 204, 216, 228, each montage cut (252, 264, 276, 288, 300, 312, 324), 456, 588, 612 and 708; the three-note sign-off at 672. Measure it and set the gain for about −16 LUFS (the reference sits at −21.6).
teaches: Paint reads as paint when every flat shape carries its own brush direction and a dry edge; and when the transitions are themselves painting (a stroke that paints the next scene on, a round window that already holds it), the cuts stop being edits and become part of the picture.

portable.fonts: Instrument Serif (400) for the one end title
portable.style: An opaque-gouache picture book, animated. Every shape is a flat, opaque patch of paint on warm paper: a slightly irregular edge, a fine streak texture running in the shape's own brush direction (across a sky, down a coat, round a hat), a few lighter streaks where the brush was full, and short dry hairs trailing off one edge. Value comes from one flat shadow shape on the side away from an upper-left light and one pale highlight dab, never from a gradient. Black is used sparingly, as dry-brush marks that taper at both ends and break into bristle streaks where the brush ran dry, only on shadow sides and defining lines, and no outline ever fully closes. Pictures change 18 times a second (every fourth frame repeats the last), which gives hand-painted motion its slight stutter. The story is original: a small kid in a mustard knitted hat with a red pom-pom, a blue duffel coat and a red scarf stands on a grey, drizzly street holding a snow globe with a lighthouse inside. Shaking it paints the world over: three broad brush ribbons sweep across and wherever they pass the street becomes the sea and the lighthouse, and the scarf streams in the wind. The globe then shows the next world before it happens: in a montage the kid stands still with the globe held high while the world behind cuts on every beat through dunes, jungle, night pines, a reef, rooftops, the moon, balloon fields and all of them at once. The camera pushes through the glass into a tiny snowy square, where the kid's giant face peers in through the curved glass and taps it; the colour lifts off to the bare ink drawing and is painted back as evening; the camera pulls back out to the kid's own street, now dry, with snow on the hat; inside the globe is that same street with a tiny kid holding a tiny globe. A brush-edged iris closes onto the globe on black and the one line of text appears: 'Shake for Elsewhere.'
portable.sound: a driving 120 bpm loop whose drums enter at the montage, a hit on the first jolt, the lighthouse landing, the end of the montage, the tap on the glass, the repaint and the closing iris; whooshes into each brush sweep, each push through the glass and the iris; soft ticks for jolts, blinks and every montage cut; a three-note sign-off.
portable.sizes: re-stack it for vertical: the kid's face above and the globe held larger below, worlds painted taller, brush ribbons sweeping diagonally, a taller montage figure with the globe in the top third, and the end title on two centred lines.
